question.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the section of the polar curve $r=\sqrt{3}\,$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}?$
question.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & ={(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}-{(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2} \\  & =3{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -3{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =3({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\sqrt{3})=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{(\sqrt{3})}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}3\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta \cdot \sqrt{3}\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =3\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$
